title: Capstone Part 3: Deployment and Reporting
summary: A model that only lives in your notebook can't demonstrate impact, so Part 3 turns your capstone into a shareable product and a compelling story, the parts that most impress employers and stakeholders. First, you package your trained model and build
content:
# Capstone Part 3: Deployment and Reporting ##### The link that got the interview A hiring manager in Bengaluru described how she screens data science applications. She opens the GitHub link, scans the README for thirty seconds, and looks for a live demo URL. If there is one and it loads, the candidate goes on the shortlist. If there is no README or the notebook is the only artifact, she moves on. She estimated she does this for around sixty applications per role and reaches the shortlist in about twenty minutes. Two candidates in one recent round had comparable models. One submitted a repository with eleven notebooks and no README. The other submitted a repository with a two-paragraph summary, a results table, a working Streamlit link, and a three-minute video. She interviewed the second candidate and never opened the first repository's notebooks. The analysis was similar. The **packaging** was not. Part 3 is the day that converts two days of technical work into something that produces opportunities, and it is the day most people skip because it feels less like real work. ##### Packaging the model Yesterday you saved the fitted pipeline. Today, make it genuinely portable. ```python import joblib, json, sklearn, datetime from pathlib import Path Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True) joblib.dump(final_pipeline, "models/pipeline.joblib", compress=3) metadata = { "model_name": "churn-predictor", "version": "1.0.0", "trained_at": datetime.datetime.now().isoformat(), "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__, # MUST match at load time "python_version": "3.12", "numeric_features": num_cols, "categorical_features": cat_cols, "feature_order": list(X_train.columns), # order matters "categories": {c: sorted(X_train[c].dropna().unique().tolist()) for c in cat_cols}, # for dropdown options "threshold": float(threshold), "metrics": {"test_pr_auc": 0.341, "test_roc_auc": 0.824, "precision_at_200": 0.615}, "training_rows": len(X_train), "data_window": "2024-01-01 to 2025-12-31", "known_limitations": [ "Weak on accounts under 30 days old (recall 0.31)", "Excludes B2B accounts", "Correlational, not causal", ], } Path("models/metadata.json").write_text(json.dumps(metadata, indent=2)) print(f"model size: {Path('models/pipeline.joblib').stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB") ``` The metadata is doing three jobs. It records the **environment** so a version mismatch is detectable rather than silent. It carries the **feature contract** — names, order, and valid category values — so the app can build correct inputs. And it carries the **limitations** so they appear in the interface rather than only in your report. Add a smoke test that runs before you deploy anything: ```python def smoke_test(model_path="models/pipeline.joblib"): model = joblib.load(model_path) meta = json.load(open("models/metadata.json")) sample = X_test.head(5)[meta["feature_order"]] probs = model.predict_proba(sample)[:, 1] assert len(probs) == 5 and ((probs >= 0) & (probs <= 1)).all() print("smoke test passed:", probs.round(4)) smoke_test() ``` That five-line function catches the most common deployment failure — a saved model that cannot actually be loaded and used in a fresh process. ##### Building the app ```python # app.py import streamlit as st import pandas as pd, joblib, json st.set_page_config(page_title="Churn Risk", page_icon="📊", layout="centered") @st.cache_resource def load(): return joblib.load("models/pipeline.joblib"), json.load(open("models/metadata.json")) model, meta = load() st.title("Customer Churn Risk Predictor") st.caption(f"Model v{meta['version']} · trained {meta['trained_at'][:10]} · " f"test PR-AUC {meta['metrics']['test_pr_auc']}") tab_single, tab_batch, tab_about = st.tabs(["Single customer", "Batch upload", "About"]) with tab_single: with st.form("predict"): c1, c2 = st.columns(2) with c1: tenure = st.number_input("Tenure (months)", 0, 240, 12) monthly = st.number_input("Monthly charges (₹)", 0.0, 100_000.0, 1200.0, 50.0) logins = st.number_input("Days since last login", 0, 365, 7) with c2: contract = st.selectbox("Contract", meta["categories"]["contract_type"]) payment = st.selectbox("Payment method", meta["categories"]["payment_method"]) tickets = st.number_input("Support tickets (30d)", 0, 50, 0) go = st.form_submit_button("Predict", type="primary", use_container_width=True) if go: row = pd.DataFrame([{ "tenure_months": tenure, "monthly_charges": monthly, "days_since_login": logins, "contract_type": contract, "payment_method": payment, "support_tickets": tickets, }])[meta["feature_order"]] # Validation before prediction warnings = [] if tenure > 120: warnings.append("Tenure beyond 10 years is outside the training range.") if tenure < 1: warnings.append("Model is weak on accounts under 30 days " f"(recall {0.31}). Treat with caution.") for w in warnings: st.warning(w) prob = float(model.predict_proba(row)[0, 1]) left, right = st.columns([1, 2]) left.metric("Churn probability", f"{prob:.1%}") with right: if prob >= 0.60: st.error("**High risk** — prioritise for retention outreach") elif prob >= meta["threshold"]: st.warning("**Moderate risk** — include in the next campaign") else: st.success("**Low risk** — no action needed") st.progress(prob) with st.expander("How to interpret this"): st.markdown(f""" Estimated probability of cancellation within 90 days, based on {meta['training_rows']:,} historical customers. | Range | Action | |---|---| | Above 60% | High risk — contact now | | {meta['threshold']:.0%}–60% | Moderate — next campaign | | Below {meta['threshold']:.0%} | Low — no action | This is a statistical estimate, not a certainty. It should inform a decision, not make one. """) with tab_batch: up = st.file_uploader("Upload a CSV", type="csv") if up: batch = pd.read_csv(up) missing = set(meta["feature_order"]) - set(batch.columns) if missing: st.error(f"Missing columns: {sorted(missing)}") else: batch["churn_probability"] = model.predict_proba( batch[meta["feature_order"]])[:, 1] batch = batch.sort_values("churn_probability", ascending=False) st.dataframe(batch.head(100), use_container_width=True) st.download_button("Download scored CSV", batch.to_csv(index=False), "scored.csv", "text/csv") st.caption(f"Top 200 customers by risk capture an estimated " f"{meta['metrics']['precision_at_200']:.0%} true churners.") with tab_about: st.markdown(f""" ### About this model **Data:** {meta['training_rows']:,} customers, {meta['data_window']} **Performance:** PR-AUC {meta['metrics']['test_pr_auc']} (baseline 0.089), precision@200 {meta['metrics']['precision_at_200']} **Known limitations:** """ + "\n".join(f"- {l}" for l in meta["known_limitations"])) ``` Three deliberate choices. **Tabs** separate the single-prediction, batch and documentation use cases instead of one long scroll. **The limitations from metadata appear in the interface**, so a user cannot miss them. And the **batch tab with a download button** is what makes this genuinely useful to an operations team rather than a toy. ##### Deploying ```bash pip freeze > requirements.txt # pin everything, especially scikit-learn # .gitignore should exclude data/raw/, .venv/, .env git add app.py requirements.txt models/ src/ notebooks/ README.md .gitignore git commit -m "Add Streamlit app and deployment artifacts" git push origin main ``` Then connect the repository at `share.streamlit.io`, point it at `app.py`, and deploy. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Trained pipeline
+ metadata] --> B[app.py with
validation + interpretation] B --> C[Test locally
streamlit run app.py] C --> D[Pinned requirements.txt] D --> E[Push to GitHub] E --> F[Streamlit Cloud] F --> G[Public URL in README,
CV, LinkedIn] ``` Practical notes that determine whether it works: **pin `scikit-learn` exactly**, because a version mismatch between training and serving is the most common deployment failure. **Commit the model file** if it is under about 50 MB. Free-tier apps **sleep after inactivity** and take roughly 30 seconds to wake, which is worth mentioning if you put the link on a CV. And never deploy real confidential data to a public URL. Test the deployment from a different device, on mobile data, in an incognito window. A link that only works on your machine is worse than no link. ##### The project report The report is what a technical reviewer reads. Structure it so someone can stop after any section and still have gained something. ```markdown # Customer Churn Prediction — Project Report ## Executive summary Churn costs approximately ₹4.2 crore annually. A LightGBM model identifies at-risk customers with precision@200 of 0.62 against a base rate of 0.089 — a 7× improvement in targeting efficiency. Deployed as a web app, it enables the 11-person retention team to prioritise their 200 monthly calls, with an estimated **₹41 lakh annual saving**. ## 1. Problem The retention team can contact ~200 customers per month out of 24,000 at-risk accounts. The current rule (30 days inactive) achieves 0.147 PR-AUC. The question is not "who will churn" but "which 200 should we call". ## 2. Data Source, size, window, and quality issues found in EDA — including the three that materially affected the analysis. ## 3. Method Splitting strategy and why (grouped by customer_id — the same customer appeared in 3.2 rows on average). Feature engineering rationale. Model progression from baseline. Cross-validation setup. ## 4. Results [The comparison table and test-set table from Part 2, with baselines.] [Business translation in rupees.] ## 5. Error analysis [The failure-mode table — this section is often the most discussed.] ## 6. Interpretation Top drivers with direction, and how they align with domain expectation. ## 7. Limitations Honest, specific, and quantified where possible. ## 8. Recommendations 1. Deploy for the monthly prioritisation workflow (ready now). 2. Run a 6-week A/B test on the intervention before claiming causal impact. 3. Build a separate model for accounts under 30 days (current recall 0.31). 4. Add pricing-change events as a feature (34% of false negatives). ## Appendix Reproduction instructions, full hyperparameters, additional figures. ``` The **Recommendations** section separated from Results is what makes this a professional document. Results say what you found; recommendations say what should happen, ranked, with the honest caveat that intervention effectiveness needs an experiment. ##### The README The README is the front door and it is where most repositories fail. It has thirty seconds to work. ```markdown # Customer Churn Prediction **[▶ Try the live app](https://churn-predictor.streamlit.app)** · [Full report](reports/report.md) · [3-min demo video](https://...) Identifies which customers to prioritise for retention outreach when capacity is limited to 200 calls per month. **Result:** precision@200 of 0.62 vs a 0.089 base rate — a 7× improvement in targeting efficiency, worth an estimated ₹41 lakh annually. ![Dashboard screenshot](reports/figures/app.png) ## Results | Model | PR-AUC | Precision@200 | |---|---|---| | Baseline (prevalence) | 0.089 | 0.089 | | Current business rule | 0.147 | 0.21 | | Logistic regression | 0.281 | 0.48 | | **LightGBM (final)** | **0.341** | **0.62** | ## Approach 1. **EDA** — found a unit inconsistency affecting 11% of rows, plus a leakage feature recorded post-decision. 2. **Features** — behavioural aggregates, tenure bands, recency signals. 3. **Modelling** — baseline → logistic → RF → tuned LightGBM, grouped CV. 4. **Deployment** — Streamlit app with single and batch prediction. ## Reproduce ```bash git clone https://github.com/you/churn-prediction.git cd churn-prediction python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt python -m src.train --config conf/default.yaml # ~90 seconds streamlit run app.py ``` Runs on the 2,000-row sample in `data/sample/`. Full data is confidential. ## What I got wrong My first split was random, which leaked customers across train and test and inflated ROC-AUC from 0.61 to 0.94. Switching to `GroupShuffleSplit` on `customer_id` gave the honest number and changed the whole project. ## Limitations - Correlational; intervention impact requires an A/B test. - Recall of 0.31 on accounts under 30 days old. - Excludes B2B accounts. ``` The **"What I got wrong"** section is the single highest-signal thing you can include. Almost nobody does it, and it demonstrates engineering judgement more clearly than any metric. Interviewers consistently ask about it. Also note: the demo link is in the first line, results appear before method, and the reproduce commands are copy-pasteable and actually tested. ##### The presentation Three to five slides, following the narrative arc from day 33. ``` 1. HOOK "Churn costs ₹4.2 crore a year. We can only call 200 customers a month." 2. INSIGHT "The current rule finds churners at 21% precision. We can reach 62%." [one chart: precision@k curve] 3. HOW "A model trained on 84,000 customers, using login recency, support history and contract type." [feature importance] 4. IMPACT "₹41 lakh annual saving. Live now at [URL]." [app screenshot] 5. NEXT "A/B test the intervention before claiming causal impact." ``` One message per slide, the title *is* the message, and everything technical goes in an appendix. Record a three-minute video walking through the live app — it costs twenty minutes and it is what people actually watch. ##### The final checklist ``` Repository [ ] README with demo link, results table, screenshot in the first screen [ ] Reproduce section with tested commands [ ] "What I got wrong" section [ ] Sample data committed so the repo actually runs [ ] Clean commit history with meaningful messages [ ] .gitignore excluding .venv, raw data, secrets [ ] Pinned requirements.txt Deployment [ ] App live at a public URL, tested from another device [ ] Input validation with clear messages [ ] Predictions interpreted, not raw probabilities [ ] Limitations visible in the interface [ ] Batch upload with CSV download Documentation [ ] Full report with executive summary and recommendations [ ] Error analysis with a failure-mode table [ ] Limitations stated and quantified [ ] 3-5 slide deck and a short demo video ``` ##### Common mistakes - Treating deployment as optional and leaving the model in a notebook. - A README with only the project title. - Method before results, so the reader never reaches the finding. - No live link, or a link that has gone stale. - Unpinned `scikit-learn`, so the deployed app fails to load the model. - No sample data, so nobody can run the repository. - Raw probabilities shown with no interpretation. - No limitations section anywhere. - Never testing the deployment from another device. - Reproduce instructions that were never actually followed. ##### Hands-on Deploy your capstone model as a Streamlit app with a public URL: single-prediction form with validation, batch upload with CSV download, an interpretation section, and the limitations from your metadata surfaced in the interface. Test it from a different device. Then draft the structured project report covering problem, data, method, results, error analysis, limitations and recommendations. For the mini-project, complete the capstone: a deployed and publicly accessible app, a polished README following the structure above with a working demo link and a "what I got wrong" section, a full report, and a three-to-five slide deck telling the data story. Commit everything to a professional GitHub repository, then run the ultimate test — clone your own repository into a fresh directory, follow your own reproduce instructions exactly, and confirm they work. Whatever breaks is what a reviewer would have hit. For the assignment, write the executive summary: one page stating the problem, the key finding and the recommendation, aimed at a non-technical decision-maker. Lead with the number that makes them care, and end with a specific ask. If it takes longer than ninety seconds to read, it is too long. ##### Key takeaways - A working demo URL in the first line of your README is what converts a project into an interview. - Save the pipeline with metadata carrying the feature contract, versions and limitations — then smoke-test loading it. - Surface limitations in the app interface, not only in the report; interpret probabilities into actions. - Lead the README and report with results, not method, and include a "what I got wrong" section. - Clone your own repository and follow your own instructions — untested reproduce steps are the most common failure.
